lecture.title: Gallbladder and Biliary Tree I: Anatomy, Investigations, Congenital Anomalies and Gallstones
golden_tip: Biliary colic = NEGATIVE Murphy's sign, no fever, normal WBC and LFT. Positive Murphy's sign with low-grade fever and leukocytosis means acute cholecystitis: admit, treat with antibiotics and plan cholecystectomy.
Only 10-20% of gallstones are radio-opaque on plain X-ray, so a normal plain film never excludes stones. Ultrasound is the prime, standard, quick and non-invasive first test.

Every choledochal cyst is premalignant (cholangiocarcinoma risk). Treatment is complete surgical excision with Roux-en-Y biliary digestive anastomosis, never simple drainage. Todani Type I (fusiform) is the most common.

A neonate with progressive jaundice since birth, pale meconium and dark urine has extrahepatic biliary atresia until proven otherwise. Operate early with Roux-en-Y anastomosis or transplant; post-op cholangitis occurs in 40% and portal hypertension in 50%.

Female, Fatty, Fertile, Forty. Mixed/cholesterol stones: 80% in US and Europe; pigment stones: 80% in Asia. Brown pigment stones form in DUCTS from stasis + infected bile (stents, parasites); black stones in the GALLBLADDER from hemolysis (SCA, spherocytosis, cirrhosis).

concepts.title: Surgical Anatomy and Physiology of the Gallbladder and Biliary Tree
concepts.summary_ar: تشريح المرارة والشجرة الصفراوية: المرارة كمثرية الشكل بطول 7.5-12 سم وسعة تتجاوز 50 مل، بأربعة أجزاء: القاع والجسم والعنق والقمع. تتحد القناة الكيسية (2.5 سم) مع القناة الكبدية المشتركة (2.5 سم) لتشكلا القناة الصفراوية المشتركة (7.5 سم). الشريان الكيسي يتفرع من الكبدي الأيمن مع خطر التفافة الشريان المتعرجة أمام منشأ القناة الكيسية، والتصريف اللمفاوي عبر عقدة لوند ثم العقد البطنية أو مباشرة إلى الكبد. الصفراء 97% ماء ويفرزها الكبد بمقدار 40 مل بالساعة، ووظائف المرارة ثلاث: خزان، وتركيز 5-10 أضعاف، وإفراز 20 مل مخاطين يومياً.

sections.heading: Gross Anatomy of the Gallbladder
sections.body_text: This first lecture of the gallbladder and biliary tree block (delivered by Dr Noori Hanoon, Consultant General and Gastrointestinal Surgeon, FRCS, FACS, FICMS and PhD (England)) covers the anatomy of the gallbladder and bile ducts, the investigations of the biliary tract, congenital anomalies, the choledochal cyst, and gallstone types, aetiology, effects and complications. The gallbladder itself is a **pear-shaped** hollow organ that lies on the under-surface of the right lobe of the liver, roughly at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage. It measures **7.5 - 12 cm in length** and has a **capacity of more than 50 ml**. Its parts, from distal to proximal, are the **fundus, body, neck and infundibulum**: the fundus is the rounded blind end that contacts the anterior abdominal wall; the body is the main storage sac; the neck is the narrowed tapered end that turns toward the porta hepatis; and the infundibulum is the funnel-shaped dilatation of the neck (Hartmann's pouch in standard descriptions) where gallstones classically impact and obstruct the cystic duct. These measurements are favorite anatomy vignette facts: a normal gallbladder is 7.5 - 12 cm long, holds more than 50 ml, and a stone trapped in the neck or infundibulum is the anatomical basis of biliary colic and mucocele.
key_points: Pear-shaped organ, 7.5 - 12 cm long, capacity more than 50 ml
Four parts: fundus, body, neck and infundibulum (Hartmann's pouch of the neck)
Stones impact at the neck/infundibulum, producing biliary colic and mucocele
The gallbladder lies on the under-surface of the liver at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage

sections.heading: The Duct System: Cystic Duct, Common Hepatic Duct and CBD
sections.body_text: The **cystic duct** is about **2.5 cm long** with a lumen of about **0.5 cm**; it runs from the neck of the gallbladder to join the **common hepatic duct, which is itself about 2.5 cm long**, and the union of the two creates the **common bile duct (CBD), about 7.5 cm long**. The CBD descends in the free edge of the lesser omentum, passes behind the first part of the duodenum and through the head of the pancreas, and opens on the ampulla of Vater beside the pancreatic duct. The triangle bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the under-surface of the liver (Calot's triangle, more accurately the hepatocystic triangle) is the crucial dissection plane during cholecystectomy: it contains the cystic artery, the cystic lymph node of Lund and sometimes an accessory hepatic duct. Memorise the three numbers together - cystic duct 2.5 cm, common hepatic duct 2.5 cm, CBD 7.5 cm - because they are classic examination facts and the landmarks of safe duct identification.
key_points: Cystic duct: 2.5 cm long, about 0.5 cm lumen
Common hepatic duct: about 2.5 cm
CBD: about 7.5 cm, formed by union of the cystic duct and common hepatic duct
Calot's (hepatocystic) triangle contains the cystic artery, the node of Lund and possible accessory ducts

check.prompt: During cholecystectomy the surgeon traces a duct 2.5 cm long that joins a common hepatic duct of similar length. What results from this junction and how long is it?
options: The common bile duct, about 7.5 cm long
The right hepatic duct, about 7.5 cm long
The common bile duct, about 12 cm long
The ampulla of Vater, about 2.5 cm long
An accessory hepatic duct, about 5 cm long
check.explanation_ar: تتحد القناة الكيسية (2.5 سم) مع القناة الكبدية المشتركة (2.5 سم) لتشكيل القناة الصفراوية المشتركة التي يبلغ طولها حوالي 7.5 سم؛ فالخيار الأول صحيح وبقية الخيارات أطوال أو تراكيب خاطئة.

sections.heading: Blood Supply and the Caterpillar Turn
sections.body_text: The gallbladder is supplied by the **cystic artery**, which arises from the **right hepatic artery** within the hepatocystic triangle and divides into anterior and posterior branches on the gallbladder wall; the vein drains into the portal system through the gallbladder bed. The anatomy is not always this tidy: the **caterpillar turn** is the name given to a **tortuous right hepatic artery that runs in front of the origin of the cystic duct, associated with a short cystic artery**. Like the crawling body of a caterpillar, the looped hepatic artery rises across Calot's triangle, and because the cystic artery arising from its apex is short, a clip or cut applied carelessly can transect or avulse the right hepatic artery itself, producing massive hemorrhage in the middle of a routine cholecystectomy. The lesson is to identify the artery entering the gallbladder wall and achieve the critical view of safety before dividing any structure.
key_points: Cystic artery arises from the right hepatic artery inside Calot's triangle
Caterpillar turn = tortuous right hepatic artery in front of the cystic duct origin with a short cystic artery
Danger: mistaking the tortuous right hepatic artery for the cystic artery causes massive bleeding

check.prompt: What exactly is the 'caterpillar turn' encountered during cholecystectomy?
options: A tortuous right hepatic artery passing in front of the origin of the cystic duct with a short cystic artery
A spiral mucosal fold inside the cystic duct (valve of Heister)
A twist of the gallbladder around its own mesentery
A redundant loop of duodenum draped over the CBD
An enlarged cystic lymph node of Lund
check.explanation_ar: التفافة الدودة هي شريان كبدي أيمن متعرج يمر أمام منشأ القناة الكيسية مصحوباً بشريان كيسي قصير؛ الخطر هو نزف كبير إذا جرح الشريان الكبدي ظناً أنه الشريان الكيسي، وبقية الخيارات تراكيب أخرى لا علاقة لها بهذا المصطلح.

sections.heading: Lymphatic Drainage of the Gallbladder
sections.body_text: The **lymphatics** of the gallbladder drain by **two ways**: **1) to the cystic lymph node (node of Lund)** at the neck of the gallbladder near the cystic duct, and from there onward to the **coeliac lymph nodes**; **2) directly to the liver** through the gallbladder bed (segments IV and V of the liver). This short, direct hepatic route explains why carcinoma of the gallbladder invades the liver substance so early, long before distant nodes are involved, and why an enlarged hard node of Lund found at laparoscopy should raise suspicion of malignancy rather than simple inflammation. For the surgeon, the node of Lund is also a practical landmark: the cystic artery usually runs just deep to it in the hepatocystic triangle.
key_points: Route 1: cystic node of Lund, then coeliac lymph nodes
Route 2: directly into the liver through the gallbladder bed
Direct hepatic spread explains early liver invasion by gallbladder carcinoma
The node of Lund is a landmark for the cystic artery plane

sections.heading: Bile: Composition, Production and the Three Gallbladder Functions
sections.body_text: **Bile is 97% water, 2% bile salts, and 1% bile acids and cholesterol.** The liver produces it continuously at about **40 ml per hour, i.e. about 1000 ml per day**; between meals the sphincter of Oddi stays closed and the bile is diverted through the cystic duct into the gallbladder. The gallbladder performs **three functions**: **1) reservoir and storage** of bile between meals; **2) concentration of bile 5 - 10 times**, by active absorption of sodium, chloride and water across its mucosa, so a small storage sac can hold the equivalent of many hours of hepatic output; and **3) secretion of mucin, about 20 ml per day**, an alkaline protective coat that shields the mucosa from the detergent action of concentrated bile salts. When a fatty meal reaches the duodenum, cholecystokinin (CCK) is released, the gallbladder contracts, the sphincter relaxes, and concentrated bile is delivered for fat digestion - the same apparatus that, when a stone blocks the neck, generates biliary colic.
key_points: Bile: 97% water, 2% bile salts, 1% bile acids and cholesterol
Production: 40 ml/hour = 1000 ml/day
Functions: reservoir and storage; concentration 5 - 10 times; mucin secretion about 20 ml/day

check.prompt: Which statement about bile composition and gallbladder function is correct?
options: Bile is 97% water, 2% bile salts and 1% bile acids plus cholesterol, produced at 40 ml/hour (1000 ml/day)
Bile is 90% water and 10% cholesterol, produced at 100 ml/hour
The gallbladder concentrates bile 50 times and secretes 200 ml of mucin daily
Bile production is 400 ml/day and the gallbladder stores it all
Bile contains no cholesterol because cholesterol is excreted only in urine
check.explanation_ar: الصفراء 97% ماء و2% أملاح صفراوية و1% أحماض صفراوية وكوليسترول، ويفرزها الكبد بمعدل 40 مل بالساعة أي 1000 مل يومياً؛ والمرارة تكثف الصفراء 5-10 مرات فقط وتفرز 20 مل مخاطين يومياً، فبقية الخيارات تخطئ الأرقام.

key_terms.definition_ar: كيس كمثري الشكل على السطح السفلي للكبد، طوله 7.5-12 سم وسعته أكثر من 50 مل، ويتألف من القاع والجسم والعنق والقمع.
قناة تخرج من عنق المرارة، طولها 2.5 سم وقطرها حوالي 0.5 سم، وتنضم إلى القناة الكبدية المشتركة لتشكيل القناة الصفراوية المشتركة.
القناة الصفراوية المشتركة؛ تتشكل من التقاء القناة الكيسية بالقناة الكبدية المشتركة، ويبلغ طولها حوالي 7.5 سم وتنتهي في أمبولة فاتر.
الشريان المغذي للمرارة، يتفرع من الشريان الكبدي الأيمن داخل مثلث كالو، ويجب ربطه بأمان قرب جدار المرارة أثناء استئصالها.
تفافة الشريان الكبدي الأيمن المتعرج أمام منشأ القناة الكيسية مع شريان كيسي قصير؛ مصدر خطر نزفي كبير أثناء جراحة المرارة.
العقدة اللمفاوية الكيسية عند عنق المرارة؛ تستقبل التصريف اللمفاوي للمرارة ثم تصرفه إلى العقد البطنية، و هي معلم مرشدي للشريان الكيسي.
مخاط تفرزه المرارة بمقدار حوالي 20 مل يومياً لحماية جدارها من فعل الأملاح الصفراوية المركزة.

concepts.title: Investigations of the Biliary Tract
concepts.summary_ar: يستعرض هذا المفهوم التحقيقات العشرة للمسالك الصفراوية: صورة البطن البسيطة ودلالاتها الأربع (حصى ظللة 10-20% فقط، مرارة خزفية، صفراء جيرية، غاز في الشجرة الصفراوية)، والدراسات المهجورة تاريخياً، والموجات فوق الصوتية كفحص أول ومعياري، والتنظير الظهاري الارتجاعي مع تنظير الموجات فوق الصوتية والتصوير عبر الجلد عبر الكبد، والرنين المغناطيسي بلا مادة ظليلة، والنظائر المشعة حيث تظهر المرارة خلال 30 دقيقة وتأخرها إلى ساعة يعني التهاب أقنية حاداً أو مرارة متقلصة، والمقطعية لتقييم الكبد والبنكرياس والعقد اللمفاوية، والتصوير والتنظير أثناء الجراحة.

sections.heading: Plain X-ray and Historical Contrast Studies
sections.body_text: A plain abdominal X-ray contributes little to gallstone diagnosis but can show four classic findings: **1) radio-opaque gallstones in only 10 - 20% of patients** (pure cholesterol stones are radiolucent; only stones with enough calcium, typically pigment stones, cast a shadow); **2) porcelain gallbladder** - a calcified gallbladder wall, itself associated with an increased risk of gallbladder carcinoma; **3) limey bile** - calcium carbonate suspended in the bile (milk of calcium) layering inside the gallbladder; and **4) gas in the biliary tree (pneumobilia)** - evidence of a biliary-enteric communication such as a cholecystoduodenal fistula with gallstone ileus, or of a previous sphincterotomy. **Oral cholecystography and intravenous (IV) cholangiography**, once the mainstay of gallstone imaging, are now **out of use and of historical interest only**, having been replaced by ultrasound and MRCP because they depended on contrast absorption and gave poor, often misleading information.
key_points: Radio-opaque stones: only 10 - 20% on plain film
Plain film may also show porcelain gallbladder, limey bile and gas in the biliary tree
Gas in the biliary tree suggests a biliary-enteric fistula (e.g. gallstone ileus)
Oral cholecystography and IV cholangiography are out of use - historical interest only

check.prompt: What proportion of gallstones are radio-opaque on a plain abdominal X-ray?
check.explanation_ar: فقط 10-20% من حصى المرارة ظللة للأشعة لأن حصى الكوليسترول النقية شفافة؛ لذلك الصورة البسيطة لا تنفي وجود الحصى أبداً، وقد تكشف بدلاً من ذلك مرارة خزفية أو صفراء جيرية أو غازاً في الشجرة الصفراوية.

sections.heading: Ultrasonography - the Prime and Standard Test
sections.body_text: **Ultrasonography is the prime test and the standard test** for the biliary tract: it is **quick, non-invasive**, uses neither radiation nor contrast, and can be repeated at the bedside in the acute patient. It demonstrates stones in the gallbladder or ducts as echogenic foci with acoustic shadowing, measures **gallbladder wall thickening** (more than 3 mm is abnormal in the fasting patient), shows **pericholecystic fluid**, gallbladder **distension**, and the diameter of the common bile duct (a duct above about 6 - 7 mm suggests obstruction, adjusting for age and after cholecystectomy), and simultaneously surveys the liver and pancreas. Its limitations are bowel gas, obesity and the poor view it gives of the distal CBD and ampulla - exactly the blind spots that MRCP and endoscopic ultrasound were designed to cover.
key_points: Prime and standard first-line test: quick and non-invasive
Shows stones, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, distension and duct diameter
Limited by bowel gas and poor visualization of the distal CBD

sections.heading: ERCP, Endoscopic Ultrasonography and PTC
sections.body_text: **ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography)** combines endoscopy and contrast radiography: the ampulla of Vater is cannulated, the ducts are outlined, and therapy is delivered in the same session - **sphincterotomy of the sphincter of Oddi, extraction of CBD stones by basket or balloon, and stent insertion** - which is why ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic; its price is a real risk of pancreatitis, bleeding and sedation complications, so it is reserved for patients who need its therapy or in whom MRCP is equivocal. **Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS)** is the most sensitive test for small common duct stones when ultrasound and LFTs disagree, and it stages periampullary tumors. **PTC (percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography)** punctures a dilated intrahepatic duct through the skin under imaging guidance: it defines the level of obstruction, allows culture of bile, and permits external biliary drainage or stenting when ERCP is impossible (for example after Roux-en-Y reconstruction or with an impacted stone the endoscope cannot pass).
key_points: ERCP = diagnostic AND therapeutic (sphincterotomy, stone extraction, stenting)
EUS: the most sensitive test for small CBD stones when ultrasound is negative
PTC: percutaneous puncture of dilated intrahepatic ducts; drainage when ERCP fails

sections.heading: MRCP - Standard Duct Imaging Without Contrast
sections.body_text: **MRCP (magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography) is the standard modality for non-invasive imaging of the ducts and requires no contrast**: stationary bile and pancreatic secretions are bright on heavy T2-weighted sequences, so the whole biliary tree and pancreatic duct are displayed in multiple planes as a 'cholangiogram without a needle'. MRCP is the test of choice for mapping duct anatomy before surgery, for classifying choledochal cysts (the Todani type), and for demonstrating strictures, duct stones and the level of obstruction in a jaundiced patient. Its drawbacks are cost, limited availability, claustrophobia and incompatibility with some implants - and it remains purely diagnostic: no biopsy, no drainage, no stone extraction can be performed through it.
key_points: Standard non-invasive duct imaging, no contrast required
Excellent for choledochal cyst typing, strictures and CBD stones
Purely diagnostic: no therapeutic option

sections.heading: Radioisotope Scanning (HIDA / IODIDA)
sections.body_text: **Radioisotope scanning uses 99mTc-labelled (labeled) HIDA or IODIDA**, injected intravenously; the tracer is taken up by hepatocytes and **excreted in bile**, so sequential gamma-camera images show hepatic uptake followed by duct, gallbladder and bowel activity. **The gall bladder is visualised (visualized) at 30 minutes**; **if visualization is delayed to 1 hour, this suggests acute cholangitis or a contracted gall bladder (chronic disease)**. Because the radiolabel follows the physiology of bile flow rather than anatomy, this is a functional test: it answers questions ultrasound cannot, such as whether the cystic duct is patent (non-visualization of the gallbladder in acute cholecystitis), whether bile is entering the intestine, and it can quantify gallbladder ejection fraction after a fatty meal or CCK stimulation in suspected chronic gallbladder dysmotility.
key_points: 99mTc-labelled HIDA or IODIDA, given IV, excreted in bile
Gallbladder normally visualized at 30 minutes
Delay to 1 hour suggests acute cholangitis or a contracted gallbladder (chronic)

check.prompt: A 99mTc-HIDA scan shows normal hepatic uptake and duct excretion, but the gallbladder is not seen until more than 1 hour after injection. What does this delay suggest?
options: Acute cholangitis or a contracted gallbladder (chronic disease)
A normal variant that needs no further test
check.explanation_ar: بحسب المحاضرة: تأخر ظهور المرارة في مسح النظائر المشعة إلى ساعة واحدة يرجح التهاب الأقنية الصفراوية الحاد أو مرارة متقلصة بسبب مرض مزمن؛ أما انعدام ظهور المرارة كلياً فيدل على انسداد القناة الكيسية في التهاب المرارة الحاد.

sections.heading: CT Scan, Per-operative Cholangiography and Choledochoscopy
sections.body_text: **CT scan** is not a first-line test for stones but is essential **to detect liver and pancreatic lesions**, to assess **cancer extent and staging**, and to reveal **lymph node enlargement** - the questions that matter once a mass or malignancy is suspected rather than simple stone disease. **Per-operative (on-table) cholangiography** injects contrast into the cystic duct (or via a catheter into the CBD) during cholecystography: it displays the duct anatomy live on fluoroscopy, confirms that the ducts are intact, and excludes or confirms CBD stones before the operation is closed. **Per-operative choledochoscopy** takes duct inspection one step further: a **flexible fibreoptic (fiberoptic) endoscope** is passed into the bile ducts **to localize and extract stones** under direct vision, inspect the mucosa, and verify clearance after extraction - the historical 'gold standard' of operative duct clearance.
key_points: CT: liver and pancreatic lesions, cancer extent and staging, lymph node enlargement
Per-operative cholangiography: on-table display of duct anatomy and stone check
Per-operative choledochoscopy: flexible fibreoptic scope to localize and extract duct stones

key_terms.definition_ar: مرارة خزفية؛ تكلّس جدار المرارة الذي يظهر كظل متكلس في الصورة البسيطة، ويرتبط بخطر متزايد لسرطان المرارة.
صفراء جيرية؛ ترسب كربونات الكالسيوم داخل الصفراء في المرارة ويظهر في صورة البطن البسيطة.
غاز في الشجرة الصفراوية يُرى في الصورة البسيطة، ويوحي بناسور بين المرارة والأمعاء كما في علوص الحصى الصفراوية.
تصوير بالنظائر المشعة بمركبات هيدا أو آيوديدا الموسومة بالتكنيشيوم 99م؛ تُعطى وريدياً وتُفرز في الصفراء فتظهر المرارة خلال 30 دقيقة.
تنظير القنوات الصفراوية والبنكرياسية بالمنظار بالطريق الارتجاعي عبر أمبولة فاتر؛ فحص تشخيصي وعلاجي معاً (قطع العاصرة واستخراج الحصى والدعامات).
تنظير بالموجات فوق الصوتية عبر المنظار؛ أدق فحص للحصى الصغيرة في القناة الصفراوية المشتركة عند الشك السريري.
تصوير القنوات الصفراوية عبر الجلد والكبد بإبرة موجهة بالأشعة، مع إمكانية تصريف الصفراء خارجياً عند فشل التنظير.
تصوير القنوات الصفراوية والبنكرياس بالرنين المغناطيسي دون مادة ظليلة؛ الفحص المعياري لرسم تشريح القنوات وتحديد نوع الكيسة القناوية.
تنظير القناة الصفراوية المشتركة بمنظار ليفي مرن أثناء الجراحة لتحديد موضع الحصى واستخراجها تحت الرؤية المباشرة.

concepts.title: Congenital Anomalies of the Gallbladder and Extrahepatic Biliary Atresia
concepts.summary_ar: تشوهات المرارة الخلقية: الغياب، والقبعة الفريجية (2-6%)، والمرارة داخل الكبد، والعائمة المعرضة للالتواء، والمزدوجة، وتشوهات القناة الكيسية (قناة إضافية، منشأ منخفض، قصيرة أو غائبة). ثم انضمور الأقنية الصفراوية خارج الكبد: يصيب 1 من كل 14000 ولادة، بتسلسل التهاب فتخريب فتليف فانسداد، وأنواعه الثلاثة بحسب مستوى الانضمور، ومظاهره السبعة من يرقان متصاعد منذ الولادة وبراز شاحن وبول داكن وإسهال دهني وكساح صفراوي وتنبع الأصابع وارتفاع ضغط الباب وتشوهات مرافقة في 20%، وتشخيصه التفريقي، وعلاجه الجراحة المبكرة بمفاغرة روا-إن-واي أو الزرع الكبدي، مع التهاب الأقنية بعد الجراحة في 40% وارتفاع ضغط الباب في 50%.

sections.heading: Congenital Anomalies of the Gallbladder
sections.body_text: The lecture lists five congenital abnormalities of the gallbladder: **1) absence of the gallbladder** (agenesis) - a rare finding; a gallbladder that 'cannot be found' at surgery or on imaging must not be assumed to have been removed until agenesis is proven. **2) Phrygian cap (2 - 6% of people)** - the fundus folds back on the body because of a **septum in the gall bladder that may be complete or incomplete**; the name comes from the folded caps worn by the people of **Phrygia (Asia Minor)**, and the anomaly is an incidental ultrasound finding of no clinical consequence in the great majority. **3) Intrahepatic gallbladder** - the organ is buried within the liver parenchyma, which makes cholecystectomy more difficult and an empyema harder to drain. **4) Floating gallbladder** - the gallbladder hangs free on a long mesentery and may undergo **torsion (volvulus)**, presenting dramatically as an acute abdomen with a tender right hypochondrial mass and requiring emergency detorsion or cholecystectomy. **5) Double gallbladder** - two gallbladders, sharing one cystic duct or draining through separate ducts; a duplicated system is prone to stasis and stone formation and is usually discovered at surgery or on imaging done for symptoms.
key_points: Phrygian cap in 2 - 6%: a septum of the fundus, complete or incomplete, named after the caps of Phrygia (Asia Minor)
Floating gallbladder can twist on its mesentery - torsion presents as an acute abdomen
Intrahepatic gallbladder complicates cholecystectomy; double gallbladder predisposes to stones
Absent gallbladder (agenesis) is rare and must be proven before assuming prior excision

check.prompt: Which congenital gallbladder anomaly classically predisposes to torsion (volvulus) of the organ?
options: Floating gallbladder hanging on a mesentery

sections.heading: Cystic Duct Anomalies
sections.body_text: The cystic duct is notoriously variable, and the lecture groups its anomalies (including intrahepatic variants of its course) into three patterns: **an accessory duct** - an accessory hepatic duct draining a segment of liver directly into the cystic duct or the gallbladder neck, the classic cause of a post-cholecystectomy bile leak when it is transected unrecognized; **low insertion** - the cystic duct descends alongside the common bile duct and joins it low, near the ampulla, so a long 'cystic duct' may be mistaken for the CBD and the junction injured; and a **short or absent cystic duct**, in which the gallbladder neck opens almost directly into the common hepatic duct, so the surgeon who clips 'the cystic duct' may in fact clip and divide the hepatic duct itself. All these variants teach the same operative doctrine: no duct is divided until the critical view of safety has been achieved and the structures entering the gallbladder have been isolated beyond doubt.
key_points: Accessory duct: classic cause of post-cholecystectomy bile leak
Low insertion: cystic duct runs down to join the distal CBD near the ampulla
Short or absent cystic duct: risk of clipping and dividing the hepatic duct
Never divide a duct before the critical view of safety is achieved

sections.heading: Extrahepatic Biliary Atresia: Frequency, Pathology and Outcome
sections.body_text: **Extrahepatic biliary atresia affects about 1 in 14000 live births.** It is an obliterative process of the **extrahepatic bile ducts over a variable length**: a progressive **inflammation, then destruction, then fibrosis, then obliteration** of the duct wall replaces the ducts with solid fibrous cords, so bile can no longer reach the intestine and instead dams back into the liver. The timing is cruel - the process advances in the weeks around birth - and the outcome of an untreated child is the outcome of progressive cholestasis: **biliary cirrhosis, portal hypertension, deepening jaundice and finally liver failure**. This natural history is the reason the differential diagnosis of prolonged neonatal jaundice is a surgical emergency: every week of delay in operating hardens the liver and halves the chance of native bile drainage.
key_points: 1/14000 live births
Occlusion of a variable length of the extrahepatic ducts
Sequence: inflammation, destruction, fibrosis, obliteration
Untreated outcome: biliary cirrhosis, portal hypertension, jaundice, liver failure

sections.heading: Types of Extrahepatic Biliary Atresia (I, II, III)
sections.body_text: Atresia is classified by the level of occlusion: **Type I - occlusion of the CBD alone. Type II - occlusion of the CBD plus the common hepatic duct. Type III - occlusion of the CBD plus the common hepatic duct plus the right and left hepatic ducts**, i.e. the entire extrahepatic tree is obliterated up to the porta hepatis. (In standard surgical series Type III is the most common form, roughly 85% of cases, and being highest it demands dissection of biliary remnants at the porta hepatis rather than a simple duct-to-bowel anastomosis, whereas Type I, the lowest, is the variant most amenable to a direct Roux-en-Y duct anastomosis.) The higher the level, the more the operation depends on finding any residual patent biliary channels at the liver hilum - the principle behind the Kasai portoenterostomy described under treatment.
key_points: Type I: occlusion of the CBD
Type II: CBD + common hepatic duct
Type III: CBD + common hepatic duct + right and left hepatic ducts (whole extrahepatic tree)
Standard series: Type III is the most common form

sections.heading: Clinical Features of Extrahepatic Biliary Atresia
sections.body_text: The clinical picture is that of a baby trapped behind an obstructed biliary tree: **1) jaundice at birth that is progressive** - conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia that deepens week by week (any jaundice persisting beyond two weeks, or urine that stains the nappy yellow, demands investigation); **2) pale meconium and pale stools** - acholic, because no bile pigment reaches the gut; **3) dark urine** - the conjugated bilirubin is excreted by the kidney instead; **4) steatorrhoea leading to osteomalacia (biliary rickets)** - without bile, fat and fat-soluble vitamin D are not absorbed, and the growing skeleton demineralises into rickets; **5) clubbing of the fingers** - a sign of chronic cholestasis in children; **6) portal hypertension** - splenomegaly, ascites and eventually variceal bleeding as cirrhosis advances; and **7) another anomaly coexists in 20% of cases** (associated anomalies, classically laterality and polysplenia syndromes, and cardiac defects).
key_points: Progressive jaundice from birth, pale meconium and dark urine
Steatorrhoea causes osteomalacia (biliary rickets)
Clubbing of the fingers and portal hypertension
Associated anomalies in 20% of cases

sections.heading: Differential Diagnosis, Treatment and Post-operative Course
sections.body_text: Four conditions make up the **differential diagnosis**: **1) neonatal jaundice** (the common physiological and haemolytic causes, which are unconjugated and self-limiting), **2) choledochal cyst** (dilatation rather than obliteration - see the next concept), **3) inspissated bile syndrome** (thick, dehydrated bile or sludge plugging otherwise normal ducts, classically after severe neonatal haemolysis), and **4) neonatal hepatitis** (intrahepatic inflammation with conjugated jaundice but patent ducts). **Treatment is early surgery: a Roux-en-Y biliary digestive anastomosis** - in practice the Kasai hepaticoportojejunostomy, in which a Roux loop is anastomosed to the cut liver surface at the porta hepatis where minute biliary remnants may still drain - **or liver transplantation** when the Kasai fails, when diagnosis has been too late, or when cirrhosis is already established. The post-operative course is guarded: **cholangitis develops in 40% of operated children** (ascending infection of the Roux limb presenting as fever and rising bilirubin) and **portal hypertension persists or develops in 50%**, so these children need lifelong hepatology follow-up, and many still come to transplantation.
key_points: DDx: neonatal jaundice, choledochal cyst, inspissated bile syndrome, neonatal hepatitis
Rx: early Roux-en-Y biliary digestive anastomosis (Kasai portoenterostomy) or liver transplantation
Post-operative: cholangitis in 40%, portal hypertension in 50%

sections.heading: Definition and Clinical Triad
sections.body_text: A **choledochal cyst is a congenital cystic dilatation of the biliary tract, particularly the common bile duct**. It presents classically in children (girls more often than boys) with a triad: **1) jaundice**, typically intermittent or fluctuating and deepening during episodes of cholangitis; **2) a right hypochondrial cystic mass** - a palpable, tense, cystic swelling beneath the right costal margin; and **3) cholangitis and pancreatitis** - recurrent attacks of fever with rigors and jaundice from infected stagnant bile, and bouts of acute pancreatitis when the dilated terminal duct or debris obstructs the pancreatic outflow. The complete triad is seen more often in children; adults more often present with complications of long-standing disease (stones, cholangitis, or even cholangiocarcinoma), which is why a choledochal cyst found in an adult is a far more sinister finding than the same cyst in a child.
key_points: Congenital cystic dilatation of the biliary tract, particularly the CBD
Triad: jaundice + right hypochondrial cystic mass + cholangitis and pancreatitis
The full triad is more typical of children; adults present with complications

sections.heading: Diagnosis and Premalignant Potential
sections.body_text: **Ultrasound is the diagnostic test**: it shows the cystic dilatation of the bile duct as a fluid-filled structure separate from the gallbladder, often with sludge or stones inside. **MRCP** is then performed to map the exact anatomy, define the extent of dilatation, assign the Todani type and plan the resection - it is the standard, contrast-free way to see the whole duct system. A choledochal cyst is **premalignant: it carries a real risk of cholangiocarcinoma**, a risk that rises with the patient's age and increases sharply after internal drainage operations that leave the diseased epithelium in place. This malignant potential, more than the symptoms themselves, dictates the treatment: excision rather than drainage.
key_points: Ultrasound = the diagnostic test; MRCP defines the anatomy and the Todani type
Premalignant: risk of cholangiocarcinoma, rising with age and after internal drainage
The malignancy risk is the reason treatment is excision, not drainage

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.body_text: **Treatment is surgical excision of the cyst with a Roux-en-Y biliary digestive anastomosis.** The dilated, diseased duct is resected completely - usually together with the gallbladder, since the cystohepatic junction is abnormal - and bile is redirected through a Roux-en-Y jejunal limb anastomosed to the healthy proximal duct or the hepatic duct confluence. Historically, simple internal drainage (cystoduodenostomy or cystojejunostomy) was performed, but it is now **abandoned**: it leaves the premalignant cyst wall behind, and the retained mucosa complicated by reflux and stasis led to recurrent cholangitis, stone formation and a high late incidence of cholangiocarcinoma. Complete excision removes the diseased epithelium and dramatically lowers - though never erases - the cancer risk, which is why even a perfectly excised patient keeps lifelong hepatobiliary surveillance.
key_points: Complete surgical excision + Roux-en-Y biliary digestive anastomosis
Simple internal drainage is abandoned: it leaves premalignant mucosa and causes cholangitis and stones
Even after excision, lifelong surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma continues

sections.heading: Todani Classification of Choledochal Cysts (the Lecture Diagram)
sections.body_text: The lecture's diagrammatic classification of choledochal cysts, illustrating five distinct types with anatomical representations of the biliary tree and gallbladder, shows: **Type I - fusiform (the most common)** - a diffuse, fusiform (spindle-shaped) dilation of the extrahepatic common bile duct, with a normal gallbladder and normal intrahepatic ducts. **Type II - true diverticulum (rare)** - the diagram depicts a saccular outpouching protruding from the side of the extrahepatic bile duct while the main ductal lumen keeps a relatively normal caliber. **Type III - choledochocele (confined to the duodenum)** - a cystic dilation localized to the intramural portion of the distal common bile duct within the duodenal wall, so the duodenum is explicitly indicated at the site of the cyst. **Type IVa - multiple (intra/extrahepatic)** - multiple cystic dilations involving both the intrahepatic bile ducts and the extrahepatic biliary tree. **Type IVb - multiple (extrahepatic only)** - multiple, separate cystic dilations confined strictly to the extrahepatic biliary system, with the intrahepatic ducts unaffected. (The complete Todani system in standard references adds **Type V - multiple intrahepatic cysts, Caroli disease** - which was not included in this lecture's five-type diagram.)
key_points: Type I fusiform: diffuse dilation of the extrahepatic CBD - the most common type
Type II true diverticulum: rare saccular side-pouch with a normal duct lumen
Type III choledochocele: cystic dilation of the intramural distal CBD confined to the duodenum
Type IVa: multiple intra- and extrahepatic dilations; Type IVb: multiple extrahepatic only
Standard references add Type V (Caroli disease, intrahepatic only), not shown in the lecture diagram

concepts.summary_ar: وبائيات حصى المرارة: أنثى، سمينة، خصبة، في الأربعين. الحصى المختلطة والكوليسترولية تمثل 80% من الحصى في أمريكا وأوروبا بينما الصباغية تمثل 80% في آسيا. الجدول الكامل يقارن أربعة أنواع من حيث الموقع والمكونات والملامح العيانية والمسببات والتوزيع الجغرافي: الكوليسترولية كبيرة مفردة بيضاء، والمختلطة الأشيع صغيرة متعددة الأوجه خضراء أو صفراء، والسوداء من الانحلال الدموي المزمن (منجلية، تكور كروي وراثي، تشمع)، والبنية من ركود الصفراء وعدواها مع الدعامات والطفيليات. ثم قائمة المسببات الخمس ومخطط الشكل 67.26 بعوامله الأربعة.

sections.heading: Epidemiology: Female, Fatty, Fertile, Forty
sections.body_text: The classical risk profile for gallstone disease is remembered as the **four Fs: Female, Fatty, Fertile, Forty**. Female - oestrogen and progesterone make bile more lithogenic and the gallbladder more sluggish; Fatty - obesity increases cholesterol secretion into bile; Fertile - each pregnancy adds progesterone-induced stasis on a supersaturated bile; and Forty - the age around which the cumulative burden declares itself. By geography the stone populations differ sharply: **cholesterol and mixed stones account for about 80% of stones in the US and Europe**, while **pigmented stones account for about 80% of stones in Asia**, a distribution driven by diet and obesity on one side and by haemolysis, cirrhosis and parasitic biliary infestation on the other.
key_points: Female, Fatty, Fertile, Forty - the classical risk profile
Cholesterol + mixed stones: 80% of stones in the US and Europe
Pigmented stones: 80% of stones in Asia

sections.heading: Cholesterol and Mixed Stones (Comparison Table, Part 1)
sections.body_text: **Cholesterol stone**: Location: **gall bladder**. Components: **hardened cholesterol - almost pure cholesterol**. Gross features: **large, solitary, white**. Common possible aetiology: **the same as for mixed stones**. World distribution: **in the US and Europe, 80% of stones are cholesterol or mixed, and around 10% of these are pure cholesterol stones**. - **Mixed stone**: Location: **gall bladder**. Components: **mostly cholesterol (51 - 99% of the stone contents) plus calcium salts, bile acids, bilirubin pigments and phospholipid**. Gross features: **small, hard, multiple, faceted, green or yellow** - the facets are polished where multiple stones have ground against each other in the gallbladder. Common possible aetiology: **the most common stone; it forms in cases in which cholesterol increases or bile acids decrease in bile - obesity, high caloric diet, contraceptive pills, ileal resection (which steals bile salts from the enterohepatic circulation) and abnormal emptying of the gall bladder (stasis)**. World distribution: **in the US and Europe, 80% of stones are cholesterol or mixed, and around 70% of these are mixed stones**.
key_points: Cholesterol stone: gallbladder; almost pure hardened cholesterol; large, solitary, white
Cholesterol stones are about 10% of US/Europe stones
Mixed stone: 51 - 99% cholesterol + calcium salts, bile acids, bilirubin pigments and phospholipid
Mixed stones: small, hard, multiple, faceted, green or yellow - the most common type (~70% of US/Europe stones)
Aetiology of both: cholesterol up or bile acids down - obesity, high caloric diet, contraceptive pills, ileal resection, abnormal gallbladder emptying

sections.heading: Black and Brown Pigment Stones (Comparison Table, Part 2)
sections.body_text: **Black pigment stone**: Location: **gall bladder**. Components: **mostly bilirubin pigments plus calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate, with up to 30% cholesterol**. Gross features: **small, black, irregular and multiple**. Common possible aetiology: **highly associated with sickle cell anaemia (anemia) (SCA), hereditary spherocytosis and cirrhosis** - chronic hemolysis overloads the bile with bilirubin, which polymerises and precipitates with calcium salts in the gallbladder. World distribution: **in the US and Europe both types of pigment stone together represent around 20% of stones, mostly in immigrant people from Asia and Africa; in Asia, 80% of stones are pigment stones, black more than brown**. - **Brown pigment stone**: Location: **bile duct** - the only stone type that forms primarily inside the ducts rather than the gallbladder. Components: **mainly calcium bilirubinate plus calcium palmitate and calcium stearate, with up to 30% cholesterol**. Gross features: **large, brown and single**. Common possible aetiology: **associated with bile stasis and infected bile due to a foreign body in the bile duct, such as a stent, or parasitic infestations such as Clonorchis sinensis or Ascaris lumbricoides** - bacteria and parasites release beta-glucuronidase, which deconjugates bilirubin so that it combines with calcium and fatty-acid soaps in the stagnant duct. World distribution: **the same pattern - in the US and Europe both pigment types represent around 20% of stones (mostly immigrants from Asia and Africa), and they are common in Asia, where 80% of stones are pigment stones (black more than brown)**.
key_points: Black pigment: gallbladder; bilirubin pigments + calcium phosphate + calcium carbonate + up to 30% cholesterol
Black pigment gross: small, black, irregular and multiple
Black pigment aetiology: SCA, hereditary spherocytosis, cirrhosis (chronic hemolysis)
Brown pigment: bile duct; calcium bilirubinate + calcium palmitate + calcium stearate + up to 30% cholesterol; large, brown, single
Brown pigment aetiology: bile stasis + infected bile + foreign body/stent + Clonorchis sinensis or Ascaris lumbricoides
Pigment stones: about 20% of US/Europe stones (mostly Asian and African immigrants); 80% of Asian stones (black more than brown)
